question_natural: What is client-side validation in the context of Bitcoin smart contracts, and how does it differ from the way a normal blockchain validates state?
gold_titles: Only the parties involved validate state transitions, off-chain, not the whole network
The blockchain stores only a cryptographic commitment, not the contract data
Contrast: normal blockchains have every node replicate/validate/store all state (global validation)
Benefits: privacy (data seen only by counterparties) and scalability (data off-chain)
Each participant keeps and verifies only their own relevant shard/history

question_natural: What is a single-use seal as defined by Peter Todd, and what are the two core operations that characterise it?
gold_titles: Cryptographic analogue of a physical tamper-evident seal; can be closed exactly once over one message
Infeasible to produce two valid closures of the same seal over different messages (uniqueness/anti-double-spend)
Two operations: Close (seal over message -> witness) and Verify (seal, witness, message -> bool)
Closing produces a publicly verifiable witness/proof of closure
Introduced by Peter Todd (2016 'Commitments and Single-Use Seals')

question_natural: How can a Bitcoin UTXO act as a single-use seal? Map the seal definition, the seal closing, and the proof of publication onto concrete Bitcoin mechanics.
gold_titles: A UTXO is globally unique and spendable only once
Seal definition = the specified UTXO/txout identified on-chain
Seal closing = spending that UTXO in a tx that commits to the message (e.g. via OP_RETURN or Taproot commitment)
Proof of publication = the confirmed spending transaction in Bitcoin's consensus/blockchain
Single-use property enforced by Bitcoin's double-spend prevention (cannot re-spend the UTXO)

question_natural: What is 'proof of publication' in the single-use-seal / client-side-validation model, and why is a publication medium essential to it?
gold_titles: Proof that a message/seal-closure was publicly published, not just privately committed
Requires a medium with global consensus properties (e.g. Bitcoin blockchain) that makes forgery/retroactive change hard
Lets third parties verify publication and that a seal was closed exactly once
Underpins client-side validation and single-use seals; prevents undetected equivocation/double-closure
Concept originates with Peter Todd; formalised in RGB/LNP-BP as the publication medium

question_natural: In the RGB protocol, what is a 'consignment' and what does a recipient do with it when receiving an asset?
gold_titles: Off-chain data bundle sent from sender to recipient to validate a transfer
Contains genesis, the DAG shard of state transitions up to the received output, and anchor/commitment proofs
Recipient validates locally (client-side): checks transitions against the schema
Recipient verifies each anchor commitment against Bitcoin and that each seal was closed exactly once (no conflicts)
No global RGB ledger; only the relevant history shard is needed

question_natural: RGB anchors commitments using two Deterministic Bitcoin Commitment schemes, Tapret and Opret. How does each work, and what determinism rule prevents an attacker from constructing an alternative commitment history in the same transaction?
gold_titles: Tapret: commitment placed in a Taproot output's script tree as a dedicated tapret leaf; looks like a normal Taproot spend (private)
Opret: commitment placed in an OP_RETURN output payload; provably unspendable but visible
DBC requires a transaction to provably contain exactly one valid commitment per scheme
Determinism rule: first OP_RETURN output (Opret) / first Taproot output (Tapret) is the only valid location
This prevents constructing alternative/conflicting commitment histories in the same transaction, keeping the seal-bound message unique

question_natural: What is AluVM, and what architectural choices make it suitable for deterministic, consensus-critical execution in RGB?
gold_titles: AluVM = Algorithmic Logic Unit VM: purely functional, register-based RISC virtual machine for deterministic portable computing
Created by Maxim Orlovsky, maintained by LNP/BP Standards Association; execution engine for RGB contracts
Register-based with NO random/addressable memory access
Pure functional: no side effects/I/O/global mutable state; reduced orthogonal instruction set
No undefined behaviour by design -> deterministic, so all client-side validators reach identical results (required for consensus)

question_natural: What is Contractum, and how does it relate to Strict Types and AluVM in the RGB stack?
gold_titles: Contractum: functional/declarative DSL for writing RGB smart contracts (work in progress)
Designed/led by Maxim Orlovsky under the LNP/BP Standards Association
Uses Strict Types formalism for data types -> fixed, deterministic, platform-independent binary encoding
Compiles to RGB schema, interfaces/implementations, genesis, contract operations
Compiles to AluVM bytecode as the execution target (high-level language -> AluVM)

question_natural: What is the Bifrost protocol in the LNP-BP/RGB ecosystem, and what problem does it solve that the standard Lightning BOLT stack does not?
gold_titles: Bifrost = extensible Lightning protocol defined by LNPBP standards (LNPBP-50 P2P, LNPBP-51 channels)
Transport/channel layer enabling RGB (and other client-side-validated protocols) over Lightning
Reuses Noise_XK/framing from BOLT-8 (as LNPBP-15/18) but uses Strict-Types encoding instead of BOLT TLV
Solves what BOLT can't: native deterministic commitments, single-use seals, Taproot/MuSig, multi-peer channels
Bifrost channels carrying these protocols cannot be downgraded to legacy BOLT channels

question_natural: What is the LNP/BP Standards Association, and what are the LNPBP standards?
gold_titles: Swiss non-profit association maintaining open standards and reference implementations for Bitcoin L2/L3 (RGB, Bifrost, etc.)
Manages the RGB consensus layer and governance
LNPBP standards = specs for Bitcoin-anchored primitives/protocols needing no Bitcoin fork, not covered by BOLTs
Examples: LNPBP-1/2/3 commitments, LNPBP-8 single-use seals, LNPBP-12 Tapret, RGB interfaces
Key people: Maxim Orlovsky (RGB/AluVM/Contractum lead) and Giacomo Zucco (early RGB)

question_natural: How does the Taproot Assets protocol (formerly Taro) issue and hold assets on Bitcoin, and what role does the Merkle-Sum Sparse Merkle Tree play? How does its approach compare to RGB?
gold_titles: Taproot Assets (Lightning Labs) commits asset state into a Taproot output via a tweaked key; on-chain it looks like a normal P2TR spend
MS-SMT = sparse Merkle tree (inclusion + non-inclusion proofs) where leaves carry amounts and nodes carry sums
Root sum = total supply, enabling supply-conservation / non-inflation proofs; asset ID derived from genesis outpoint + metadata
Also uses client-side validation: receivers verify an off-chain proof chain from genesis
Vs RGB: standardised on Taproot + MS-SMT (bip-tap) and Lightning Labs LN, whereas RGB uses AluVM/Strict Types, single-use-seal Tapret/Opret anchoring and different data structures

question_natural: Explain how ordinal theory numbers satoshis, how inscriptions embed data into a Bitcoin transaction, and why BRC-20 is described as an off-chain, indexer-based experiment rather than a formal protocol.
gold_titles: Ordinal theory (Casey Rodarmor) numbers sats by mining order; genesis block sats run 0 to 4,999,999,999; transfers tracked FIFO; Bitcoin is unaware (off-chain indexer)
Inscription = data in the witness of a Taproot script-path spend inside an OP_FALSE OP_IF ... OP_ENDIF 'envelope'
Envelope holds 'ord' identifier, content-type/MIME tag and body; branch never executes (no effect on validity) but is stored on-chain; uses segwit witness discount
BRC-20 by Domo (March 2023): JSON inscriptions with deploy/mint/transfer ops (p, op, tick, max, lim, amt)
Off-chain/indexer-based: Bitcoin enforces no BRC-20 rules; balances computed by indexers replaying inscriptions; no BIP/consensus standard, indexers can diverge

question_natural: What is a Solid Pod in Tim Berners-Lee's Solid project, and what problem is Solid trying to solve?
gold_titles: A Pod is a user-controlled personal online data store accessed over HTTP(S)
Solid decouples/separates data from the applications that use it
It targets data lock-in, silos, and lack of ownership/portability
A Pod can be hosted anywhere and owned/controlled by its user
The Pod owner is identified by a WebID that governs access

question_natural: The Solid Protocol builds its storage layer on existing W3C standards. Which HTTP interaction model does a Pod implement, and how do the two access-control mechanisms WAC and ACP differ?
gold_titles: Pods implement the W3C Linked Data Platform (LDP) over HTTP with containers and standard verbs
WAC is ACL-based with per-resource ACL resources in RDF
WAC access modes are Read, Write, Append, Control, plus inheritable/default ACLs
ACP uses Access Control Resources with Policies and Matchers
ACP grants a mode only if a policy allows and none deny; it is more expressive/context-aware

question_natural: How does Solid-OIDC extend plain OpenID Connect, and what role does DPoP play in letting a Solid client prove it is acting for a given WebID?
gold_titles: Solid-OIDC is a profile/extension of OpenID Connect / OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow
It adds a 'webid' scope and a 'webid' claim in the ID Token equal to the user's WebID
Issuer discovery uses solid:oidcIssuer triples in the WebID profile, not a fixed provider
DPoP (RFC 9449) binds tokens to a client-held key via proof-of-possession JWTs
Each request sends a fresh DPoP proof so the Pod verifies the caller holds the bound key

question_natural: In Solid-OIDC, how does a client know which OpenID Provider is allowed to authenticate a particular WebID?
gold_titles: The client dereferences the WebID URI to fetch its RDF profile document
It looks for solid:oidcIssuer (http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/terms#oidcIssuer) triples
The object of each triple names an authorised OpenID Provider for that WebID
The WebID owner controls this list, keeping issuer trust decentralised
A relying party accepts a token only if its issuer matches one listed in the profile

question_natural: What is a WebID, and why is it more than just a URL?
gold_titles: A WebID is an HTTP(S) URI identifying an agent (person, org, app, device)
Dereferencing it returns an RDF WebID Profile Document (often Turtle)
It typically uses a fragment (e.g. #me) so the URI denotes the agent node in the document
The profile holds identity/auth material such as public keys or trusted issuers
The owner controls their own identifier and profile, enabling decentralised identity

question_natural: How does WebID-TLS authentication differ from WebID-OIDC, and why did the ecosystem largely move to the latter?
gold_titles: Both yield a verified WebID URI the agent is proven to control
WebID-TLS uses mutual TLS with a client X.509 cert carrying the WebID in its Subject Alternative Name
WebID-TLS verifies the cert's public key against a key in the WebID RDF profile
WebID-OIDC works at the application layer via OpenID Connect ID Tokens
The move happened because client-certificate mTLS has poor browser/UX support while OIDC is widely deployed and lets holders pick their IdP

question_natural: What is the WebID Profile Document and what role does it play during authentication?
gold_titles: It is the RDF (typically Turtle) document returned by dereferencing the WebID
It describes the agent and links the document to the WebID node (e.g. foaf:primaryTopic)
It holds authentication material: public key(s) and/or trusted issuer(s)
In WebID-TLS it supplies the key matched against the client certificate; in OIDC it supplies solid:oidcIssuer
It is owner-controlled, making it the authoritative source of truth for the identity

question_natural: According to NIP-01, what are the fields of a Nostr event and how is its integrity and authorship guaranteed?
gold_titles: Event fields: id, pubkey, created_at, kind, tags, content, sig
pubkey is a 32-byte secp256k1 key; kind is an integer type (0 metadata, 1 text note)
id is the SHA-256 hash of the canonical serialisation [0,pubkey,created_at,kind,tags,content]
sig is a Schnorr signature over the id using secp256k1, verifiable against the pubkey
Any change alters the id/signature; NIP-01 also defines the WebSocket EVENT/REQ/CLOSE and EVENT/OK/EOSE/NOTICE messages

question_natural: What do the NIP-19 identifiers npub and nsec encode, and why must they not be used inside NIP-01 events or filters?
gold_titles: NIP-19 defines bech32 encodings for Nostr entities
npub encodes a public key; nsec encodes a private key; note encodes an event id
TLV forms (nprofile, nevent, naddr) add extra data like relay hints
They are for human display/copy-paste/QR only
They MUST NOT be used inside NIP-01 events or filters, which use canonical hex; clients convert on input

question_natural: How does the did:nostr DID method construct and resolve a DID, and how does it differ from ledger-based DID methods?
gold_titles: A did:nostr DID maps directly to a Nostr secp256k1 public key: did:nostr:<pubkey>
No registry, ledger, or minting step is required
Resolution is offline-first/deterministic: a minimal DID Document is built from the key alone
The verificationMethod uses Multikey / publicKeyMultibase, per W3C DID Core and Controlled Identifiers
Nostr relays can optionally enrich the document (kind-0 metadata) but are not required; control = holding the private key, unlike ledger-based methods

question_natural: Why does Git's commit structure give a tamper-evident audit trail of documents, and what is the limitation that leads people to anchor commit hashes externally?
gold_titles: Git is content-addressed: blobs, trees, and commits are named by cryptographic hashes
The commit graph is a Merkle DAG; a commit hashes its tree, parent(s), and metadata
Any content change or history rewrite changes hashes, making tampering detectable
Git commit timestamps are self-asserted local metadata and can be forged/back-dated
So commit or document hashes are anchored externally (e.g. a blockchain) for trusted proof-of-existence; 'Git-Mark' is a pattern name, not a Git feature

question_natural: How does OpenTimestamps use a blockchain to create a tamper-evident, trust-minimised timestamp for a document, and what exactly does the resulting proof demonstrate?
gold_titles: Only the document's SHA-256 hash is submitted; the document never leaves the user
Calendar servers aggregate many hashes into a Merkle tree and anchor the Merkle root in a Bitcoin transaction (e.g. OP_RETURN)
The .ots proof holds the hash, the Merkle path, and the attestation to a specific block
Verification recomputes the hash, walks the Merkle path, and checks the block, proving existence-before-time and tamper-evidence
Trust-minimised: relies only on the document, proof file, and public block headers; one transaction timestamps many documents

question_natural: Explain in what precise sense a Git repository is a Merkle DAG rather than merely a hash chain. Which four object types participate, how does an edge get its 'address', and why is the resulting graph necessarily acyclic?
gold_titles: Four object types: blob, tree, commit, tag
Object ID = cryptographic hash of the object's serialised content (content addressing)
Edges are hashes of target objects (Merkle links), so links are authenticated
DAG, not a chain: commits fan out to trees which fan out to blobs/sub-trees
Acyclic because content determines the hash — you cannot embed a hash of an object that embeds you

question_natural: Git supports a SHA-256 object format. In a repository created for the transition, what do the config extensions objectFormat and compatObjectFormat do, what auxiliary data structure must a SHA-256 repository store alongside its packfile, and what is the current state of interoperability with SHA-1 repositories?
gold_titles: objectFormat = the storage hash (sha256 => 64-hex object IDs); default is sha1
compatObjectFormat = a compatibility hash, must differ from objectFormat, for format-1 interop testing
SHA-256 repos store a bidirectional SHA-256<->SHA-1 name mapping beside the packfile
Objects can be named by 40-hex SHA-1 or 64-hex SHA-256 IDs
No interoperability today; SHA-256 support is experimental; old Git cannot read SHA-256 repos
Planned default switch to SHA-256 later; SHA-1 format not being deprecated

question_natural: Given that SHA-1 has been practically broken (SHAttered, 2017), why can Git still use SHA-1-named objects relatively safely today? Name the specific mechanism modern Git builds employ and describe what it actually detects.
gold_titles: Git uses hardened SHA-1 = sha1dc (collision-detecting SHA-1), not plain SHA-1, by default
sha1dc detects the disturbance-vector/message-block signatures of known SHA-1 collision attacks
It aborts instead of returning a digest when an attack pattern is seen, rejecting crafted colliding objects
Mitigates SHAttered-style identical-prefix collisions cheaply
It is a stop-gap; does not restore general collision resistance — hence the parallel SHA-256 transition

question_natural: A colleague argues that GPG- or SSH-signed Git commits (git commit -S) already prove exactly when a commit was made and therefore give a complete provenance trail. Identify the precise guarantee a signed commit provides, the field that makes the 'when' claim untrustworthy, and why an external timestamp is still needed.
gold_titles: Signed commit = key binds to the hashed commit object (tree, parents, identities, message) via the gpgsig header
Provides authenticity/integrity, verifiable with git verify-commit / git log --show-signature
The author/committer date fields are client-set and attacker-controllable — not attested by the signature
Signatures give no trusted time; back-/forward-dating is trivial
A trusted 'existed before T' needs an external anchor (OpenTimestamps/blockchain or a transparency log)

question_natural: git notes let you attach metadata to an existing commit without changing that commit's hash. Explain how notes are stored, why attaching a note leaves the annotated commit's object ID unchanged, and what this implies for using notes to carry provenance data such as a reference to an external timestamp proof.
gold_titles: A note is a blob stored in a separate notes ref (default refs/notes/commits), keyed by target object name
The commit object is not modified, so its object ID stays the same — hence notes can annotate immutable/signed commits
Notes are mutable after the fact (add/edit/remove) precisely because they are external to the commit
A signature over the commit does NOT cover its notes; the notes ref has its own hash chain
Good for carrying provenance pointers (e.g. an .ots proof ID) but the notes ref must be protected/signed separately

question_natural: OpenTimestamps claims it can timestamp an unlimited number of documents with a single Bitcoin transaction. Explain the aggregation mechanism, the role of calendar servers and their trust model, and describe precisely how the commitment reaches Bitcoin — in particular whether OpenTimestamps uses OP_RETURN or relies only on the block's transaction Merkle root.
gold_titles: Clients send only a document hash; requests in a ~1-second interval are aggregated into one Merkle tree
The tree tip is a single 32-byte digest; each client's proof is the sibling-hash path from its hash to the tip
One Bitcoin transaction thus anchors an unlimited number of documents
Calendars must anchor tips and keep proofs available, but need not be trusted — proofs verify against the blockchain
Deployed calendars embed the tip directly in an OP_RETURN output (per Peter Todd)
The block header's transaction merkleroot is the ultimate commitment; the alternative non-OP_RETURN scheme is not in the standard protocol

question_natural: Describe the git-mark tool's model for making a Git repository's history tamper-evident against a public ledger. What is the role of the 'genesis' transaction, what does invoking the mark do, and how does this differ in guarantee from Git's internal hash chain plus signed commits?
gold_titles: git-mark (`git mark`, via npm) anchors commit hashes to a supporting blockchain (Bitmark)
`git mark --genesis txid:output` binds the repo to a genesis unspent transaction, starting a mark chain
Each `git mark` creates a new tx committing to the current HEAD commit hash + metadata; block confirmation anchors it
Git's hash chain + signed commits give only internal integrity/authenticity, tamper-evident relative to another copy
A force-push can rewrite history undetectably without an external reference; the blockchain anchor removes that gap
Result: proof of existence/state against a global consensus ledger, not just within Git

question_natural: OpenTimestamps ships a Git integration that timestamps PGP-signed commits. Describe the wrapper mechanism it uses to hook into git commit -S, the git config setting that activates it, and explain the specific provenance problem this solves that an ordinary signed commit does not.
gold_titles: Integration wraps the GPG program Git calls: ots-git-gpg-wrapper (ots-git-gpg-wrapper.sh)
Activated via `git config gpg.program <wrapper>` (typically --global)
On `git commit -S` the wrapper both produces the GPG signature and creates an OTS proof anchoring to Bitcoin via calendars
A plain signed commit proves only 'key signed content', with no trustworthy time
Anchoring proves the signature existed before a given block time — crucial once a key is revoked/expired/compromised
Lets verifiers still trust signatures that pre-date a key's compromise

question_natural: In RFC 6962 (Certificate Transparency), the Merkle Tree Hash prepends a single byte before hashing at each node: 0x00 for leaves and 0x01 for interior nodes. Give the exact leaf and interior-node hash definitions, and explain the security property this domain separation provides.
gold_titles: Interior (n>1, k = largest power of two < n): MTH = SHA-256(0x01 || MTH(D[0:k]) || MTH(D[k:n]))
0x00 vs 0x01 = domain separation making leaf and interior hash inputs disjoint
No leaf hash can collide with an interior-node hash
Prevents second-preimage / tree-reshaping attacks where a leaf value mimics a child-hash concatenation
Needed because such structural ambiguity would exist even with a collision-resistant SHA-256

question_natural: Distinguish a Merkle audit path (inclusion proof) from a Merkle consistency proof in an RFC 6962 transparency log: what does each one prove, what inputs does each need, what does a Signed Tree Head contain, and what is the Maximum Merge Delay?
gold_titles: Inclusion/audit proof: sibling hashes from a leaf to the root; proves one leaf is in the tree of a given STH
Consistency proof: node hashes proving tree of size m is a prefix of tree of size n (m<=n) — append-only, nothing deleted/altered
Inclusion needs leaf hash + audit path + STH root; consistency needs two STH roots/sizes + consistency path
STH contains: tree size, root (tree-head) hash, timestamp, log signature (and log ID metadata)
MMD = log-declared max time to incorporate an accepted cert into the tree and cover it with an STH
Client verifies inclusion against an STH dated after SCT timestamp + MMD; failing MMD = misbehaviour

question_natural: Google Trillian is a general-purpose verifiable-log backend. What is a Trillian 'personality' and what three kinds of responsibility does it own that the Trillian core deliberately does not? Separately, what is a 'tile' in tile-based transparency logs and what problem does tiling address?
gold_titles: Trillian core = generic storage-backed append-only Merkle tree with inclusion/consistency proofs, no app semantics
A personality = the application layer for a specific log type on top of the core
Personality owns: (1) admission criteria (what may be logged)
(2) canonicalisation (equivalent submissions -> canonical form for de-duplication)
(3) external interface/API, ACLs, rate-limiting/DoS; maps to core ops like QueueLeaf/GetInclusionProof
A tile = a fixed-size subtree/group of Merkle hashes stored and served as one unit; tiling cuts storage/recompute/proof-serving overhead and eases mirroring

question_natural: AluVM is the RISC virtual machine that runs RGB contract validation scripts. Describe its register file and explain the concrete mechanisms by which it guarantees deterministic, exception-free execution with no undefined behaviour. In particular, what happens to a destination register on an impossible operation, what is the role of the st0 register, and how is control flow made total (no invalid jumps or instructions)?
gold_titles: A-registers: 8 blocks of 32 registers, widths 8/16/32/64/128/256/512/1024 bits
S-registers: one block of 256 registers, up to 64 KiB each; R-registers reserved for cryptography
Every register can hold an undefined/None state; impossible ops set destination to undefined instead of trapping
st0 is the boolean status register; flagged operations set st0=false on overflow/NaN/failure
Code is zero-padded to 2^16 bytes; the zero opcode means 'set st0=false and stop' -> no invalid instructions/jumps
Cycles and jumps are counted with a 2^16 limit for bounded-time execution

question_natural: LNPBP-1 defines the base cryptographic-commitment primitive used throughout RGB. Give the exact tweaked-key formula, and explain three specific design choices: why the message is authenticated with HMAC-SHA256 rather than a plain hash, what the HMAC key is, and why the standard deliberately uses no nonce.
gold_titles: T = Po + G * HMAC-SHA256(SHA256("LNPBP1") || SHA256(tag) || msg, S*)
Commits to the SUM of all unique keys in the output, not just one key
S* is the 64-byte uncompressed sum key (x||y, 0x04 prefix stripped) and serves as the HMAC key
HMAC-SHA256 chosen to prevent length-extension attacks on arbitrary-length messages
Double SHA256 tagged prefix prevents cross-protocol collision/replay
No nonce: the public-key sum already provides sufficient entropy

question_natural: LNPBP-2 embeds an LNPBP-1 commitment deterministically into a Bitcoin output's scriptPubkey. Why does it commit to the sum of ALL public keys in the script, how does it deterministically decide which key carries the commitment across arbitrary script types, and what happens for a Taproot (P2TR) output? What extra data must be kept off-chain for verification?
gold_titles: Exactly one key is tweaked, but it commits to the SUM of all original keys in the output -> deterministic singularity
Keys extracted deterministically via Miniscript parsing of the script
Procedure fails on an unresolvable pk_h to prevent multiple-commitment attacks
For P2TR the internal/intermediate key is tweaked, not the output key (else BIP-341 commitment breaks)
Verification requires an off-chain extra-transaction proof (ETP): original keys + script/taptweak reconstruction data

question_natural: LNPBP-4 lets a single Bitcoin commitment carry messages from multiple independent protocols while proving uniqueness in zero knowledge. Describe how a message is placed into the commitment buffer, how empty slots are filled, and how the scheme proves both that a given protocol's commitment is present and that no second commitment under the same protocol exists.
gold_titles: Buffer of N 32-byte slots, N >> M, capped at ~2 MB (16-bit slot count)
Each protocol has a unique 256-bit id; commitment placed at slot n = id mod N
Same-protocol-id collision on the same slot is what guarantees per-protocol uniqueness
Empty slots filled with BIP-340 tagged hash (tag 'LNPBP4:entropy') of entropy_seed||j
Final buffer committed via LNPBP-1/2 with tag 'LNPBP4'
Partial reveal proves presence; full reveal (with entropy_seed) proves absence of other commitments

question_natural: RGB anchors its MPC commitment into a Bitcoin transaction using one of two deterministic-bitcoin-commitment (DBC) schemes: Opret and Tapret. Contrast their exact on-chain form and byte sizes, and explain what the 1-byte nonce in a Tapret commitment is for.
gold_titles: Opret: 32-byte commitment in first OP_RETURN output; script = OP_RETURN OP_PUSHBYTES_32 <commit>, 34 bytes, on-chain visible
Tapret: commitment hidden in Taproot script tree for smaller footprint/better privacy
Tapret leaf is exactly 64 bytes: 29-byte fixed prefix + OP_RETURN + 33-byte push (32-byte MPC commitment + 1-byte nonce)
Tapret leaf inserted as unspendable script, shifting existing scripts down a level
Lexicographic branch ordering means left-placement needs a larger uniqueness proof
The 1-byte nonce is 'mined' so the leaf hash sorts to the right side, minimising the proof

question_natural: Single-use-seals are the anti-double-spend primitive underpinning RGB. State the abstract operations a single-use-seal implementation must provide, give the precise security property a secure implementation must satisfy, and explain how Bitcoin is used to realise a trust-minimised seal.
gold_titles: Core ops: Close(l,m)->w and Verify(l,w,m)->bool; plus Gen(p)->l and authenticated Close(l,m,s)->w
A seal can be closed over a message exactly once
Security: infeasible to make Verify true for two distinct messages on the same seal
Multiple witnesses for the same seal/message pair are acceptable (non-ideal)
Trivial impl = trusted notary with disposable keys; trust-minimised = proof-of-publication ledger (Bitcoin)
On Bitcoin, closing a seal = spending the defined UTXO with an on-chain commitment

question_natural: In RGB, data is moved between parties as 'consignments'. Distinguish a contract consignment from a transfer (terminal) consignment, explain why the two differ so much in size, and describe the role of the receiver's blinded UTXO and the 'stash' in a transfer.
gold_titles: Contract consignment = Genesis + Schema, only a few KiB
Transfer/terminal consignment = final state transition + full validated history since Genesis (hence much larger)
History is needed so the receiver can verify against Bitcoin anchors client-side
Invoice encodes a seal definition, typically the receiver's UTXO in blinded form
Stash = each party's store of client-side-validated data
Sender embeds Opret/Tapret DBC in a PSBT (plus blank transitions); receiver 'rgb accept' validates before broadcast

question_natural: RGB separates a contract 'Schema' from a contract 'Interface'. Explain what each is, how an RGB Schema differs fundamentally from an Ethereum on-chain contract, and how RGB interfaces (e.g. RGB20, RGB21, RGB25) relate to the concrete schemas an issuer uses.
gold_titles: Schema = declarative template (like a class): owned/global state, assignments, transitions, metadata, embedded AluVM validation scripts
Issuer instantiates a schema in Genesis (ticker, precision, issued supply, allocations); compiled to .rgb/.rgba
Unlike Ethereum, the RGB contract is declarative and validated client-side; only a commitment goes on Bitcoin
Interfaces (v0.10+) are ABI/ERC-like APIs but bundled with the contract, needing no separate standardisation/distribution
Multiple interfaces can be added to an immutable contract over time
RGB20 = fungible (NIA), RGB21 = unique/NFT (UDA), RGB25 = collectible fungible (CFA)

question_natural: RGB's consensus data is represented with 'Strict Types' rather than a conventional serialization. What distinguishes strict types from algebraic data types in languages like Haskell, what is the 64 KiB rule, and why does RGB compile its whole consensus layer into strict types?
gold_titles: Formal, deterministic notation for ADTs targeting real platforms, not abstract theory
Every collection has explicit min/max bounds baked into the type -> compile-time resource prediction, no runtime exceptions
Determinism: differing byte sequences always mean semantically distinct data
64 KiB rule: no atomic encoded piece may exceed 64 KiB, enabling embedded/limited-memory use
Enables formal verification of (de)serialization and memory-layout equivalence
RGB compiles its whole consensus layer to strict types for binary-compatibility proofs across releases; by Orlovsky/UBIDECO

question_natural: Bifrost (LNPBP-50, with LNPBP-51 and LNPBP-53) is proposed as a replacement/extension networking layer for Lightning, in part to carry RGB data. Why did the LNP/BP designers introduce a new protocol instead of extending the BOLTs, what encoding change is central to it, and what do LNPBP-51 and LNPBP-53 add on top of the LNPBP-50 core?
gold_titles: Extending BOLTs is hard: features span multiple standards, no isolation of experimental code, payment-only design
BigInt encoding in BOLTs is unsuitable for client-side-validated data -> Bifrost uses strict encoding for all fields
LNPBP-50 = generalized core: TCP, dedicated default port 9913, Noise_XK (LNPBP-15) + framing (LNPBP-18), bifrost:// URLs, local-features flag
LNPBP-51 = channel-management protocol
LNPBP-53 = multi-peer payment channels for Bifrost
LNPBP-35 (related) carries RGB data propagation over Lightning

question_natural: Carbonado is the archival storage format associated with RGB wallet stash persistence (notably in BitMask). It is described as 'apocalypse-resistant data storage for the truly paranoid'. What combination of cryptographic and coding techniques does it layer into a single flat-file container, and what problem is each layer solving?
gold_titles: Single flat-file archival container for long-term consensus-critical data (e.g. RGB stash), used by BitMask
Authenticated encryption (v2: AES-256-CTR + HMAC-SHA512 encrypt-then-MAC) for confidentiality + integrity
Bao (BLAKE3-based) verified streaming with per-4 KiB-slice verifiability
Reed-Solomon forward error correction (deterministic 4/8) against bit-rot / partial loss
Optional Zstandard compression; optional post-quantum SLH-DSA (FIPS-205) signature sidecars
Purpose: private, verifiable, recoverable data because losing client-side history loses the RGB asset

question_natural: In the did:nostr DID method, what exactly is the method-specific identifier, and what does a resolver produce in the minimal (offline) resolution tier? Specifically, name the verification method type and the two verification relationships that must reference it, and describe how the publicKeyMultibase value is built from the Nostr key.
gold_titles: Method-specific id = 64-char lowercase hex x-only secp256k1 pubkey; npub is display-only
Minimal document is derived offline from the key alone, with type "DIDNostr"
Verification method type is "Multikey"; authentication and assertionMethod both reference #key1
publicKeyMultibase = 'f' (base16 multibase) + e701 (secp256k1 multicodec) + parity byte + hex key
Three-tier resolution: minimal (offline) -> HTTP .well-known/did/nostr/<pubkey>.json -> enhanced relay query (kind 0/3/10002); no dedicated DID-document event kind

question_natural: How does NIP-05 map a name@domain identifier to a Nostr public key? Give the exact HTTP request a client makes, the structure of the JSON returned, the meaning of the special '_' name, and the core security rule about what a client must actually follow.
gold_titles: Request: GET https://<domain>/.well-known/nostr.json?name=<local-part>
JSON has required 'names' (name -> lowercase hex pubkey) and optional 'relays' (pubkey -> [relay URLs])
'_' is the root identifier, displayed as the bare domain name
Security rule: clients follow the pubkey, never the NIP-05 address as primary identity
No redirects allowed; CORS header Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * recommended

question_natural: What is the NIP-07 window.nostr capability, and what problem does it solve for Nostr web apps? Name the two mandatory methods and their signatures, describe what signEvent receives and returns, and list the optional encryption namespaces.
gold_titles: window.nostr is injected by an extension/signer so the private key never reaches the web page
getPublicKey(): returns hex pubkey
signEvent(event) takes {created_at, kind, tags, content} and returns it with id, pubkey, sig added
Optional nip04 (deprecated) and nip44 encrypt/decrypt namespaces
getRelays() optional; extension injected at document_end

question_natural: NIP-19 defines both bare bech32 entities (npub, nsec, note) and TLV-carrying ones (nprofile, nevent, naddr). Which bech32 variant does it use, and what are the four TLV type numbers and their meanings? Explain concretely how an nprofile differs from an npub and what data an naddr must carry.
gold_titles: Uses bech32, explicitly NOT bech32m
Bare npub/nsec/note are hex re-encoded; nprofile/nevent/naddr carry TLV
TLV type 0 = special (pubkey / event id / identifier string depending on prefix)
TLV type 1 = relay (ASCII URL, repeatable); type 2 = author (32-byte pubkey); type 3 = kind (32-bit big-endian)
nprofile = pubkey + relay hints (vs bare npub); naddr must carry identifier + author + kind

question_natural: Describe the NIP-42 challenge-response authentication flow between a Nostr client and a relay. What event kind is used, which two tags must it contain, what does the relay validate, and how does a relay signal that a request needs authentication?
gold_titles: Relay sends ["AUTH", challenge]; client returns ["AUTH", signed event]
Event is ephemeral kind 22242, never broadcast
Required tags: ["relay", url] and ["challenge", string]
Relay checks kind=22242, created_at within ~10 min, challenge match, relay URL match
'auth-required: ' prefix signals need to authenticate; 'restricted: ' for insufficient permission

question_natural: What is a NIP-65 relay list, and how does it enable the 'outbox' (gossip) model? Give the event kind, the tag used to list relays, the meaning of the read/write markers including an unmarked entry, and the rule for where a client should look to fetch a given user's posts versus their mentions.
gold_titles: kind 10002, replaceable, uses 'r' tags with relay URLs
Markers 'read' and 'write'; omitted marker means both
Fetch a user's posts from their WRITE relays; send mentions/replies to their READ relays
Underpins the outbox/gossip model (spread load onto authors' own relays)
Keep list small (~2-4 per category); propagate widely / to indexers

question_natural: In Solid-OIDC, how is a user's WebID conveyed and how does a resource server avoid trusting a rogue OpenID Provider that issues tokens for arbitrary WebIDs? Also explain the two Solid-OIDC features that remove the need for pre-registered clients and for bearer tokens, and how a DPoP proof (RFC 9449) is bound to the access token.
gold_titles: ID Token carries webid claim, plus azp and aud including azp and 'solid'
WebID Provider Confirmation checks solid:oidcIssuer triple (http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/terms#oidcIssuer) so issuer matches WebID-authorised OP
Client ID is a dereferenceable Client ID Document (JSON-LD), removing static registration
DPoP proof JWT (RFC 9449): header typ=dpop+jwt/alg/jwk, claims jti/htm/htu/iat (+ath with a token)
Access token cnf.jkt = base64url SHA-256 JWK thumbprint binds the token to the client's DPoP key, preventing bearer-style replay

question_natural: Contrast Solid's two authorization systems, WAC and ACP. For WAC, name the authorization modes, the difference between acl:accessTo and acl:default, and how public access is granted. For ACP, name the core resource and objects (ACR, policy, matcher) and the boolean combinators, and state the key conceptual capability ACP adds that WAC lacks.
gold_titles: WAC modes: acl:Read, acl:Write, acl:Append, acl:Control (Control = over the ACL itself)
acl:accessTo = this resource; acl:default = on a container, inherited by contained resources lacking their own ACL
Public via acl:agentClass foaf:Agent; acl:AuthenticatedAgent = any logged-in agent; ACL found via Link rel=acl
ACP: ACR -> acp:AccessControl -> acp:Policy (acp:allow/acp:deny) gated by acp:Matcher via acp:allOf/anyOf/noneOf
ACP adds attribute/context conditions on acp:client, acp:issuer and acp:vc, not just agent identity

question_natural: Explain how WebID-TLS authenticates an agent using a client certificate and the WebID profile document, naming the certificate field that carries the WebID and the RDF ontology terms a verifier matches the certificate key against. Then give the main reasons the Solid community moved from WebID-TLS to WebID-OIDC / Solid-OIDC.
gold_titles: WebID-TLS: WebID is carried in the certificate's SubjectAlternativeName (URI)
Verifier dereferences WebID profile and matches key via cert:key -> cert:RSAPublicKey with cert:modulus (hexBinary) and cert:exponent (integer)
TLS handshake proves private-key possession; key match binds cert to WebID
Moved away due to poor browser client-cert UX: confusing dialogs, no logout, multi-identity/shared-machine problems, weak mobile/browser support
Solid-OIDC keeps WebID but uses OAuth2/OIDC token flow plus WebID Provider Confirmation

question_natural: In the Solid Notifications Protocol, how does a client subscribe to changes on a resource, and what are the two standard channel types? Give their exact type identifiers and namespace, the property used to name the resource of interest, and the response property that differs between the WebSocket and Webhook channels.
gold_titles: Subscribe via authenticated POST of JSON-LD (context .../solid/notification/v1) to the subscription resource
Channel types in namespace http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/notifications#
WebSocketChannel2023 and WebhookChannel2023
notify:topic names the target resource; WebSocket response gives notify:receiveFrom; Webhook request supplies notify:sendTo
Notifications are Activity Streams 2.0 JSON-LD

question_natural: How does OpenTimestamps let thousands of documents be timestamped by a single Bitcoin transaction, and what does a .ots proof actually contain? Describe the role of calendar servers, the two-step stamp-then-upgrade workflow, the kinds of operations and attestations inside a proof, and how verification recomputes the path to Bitcoin.
gold_titles: Calendar servers aggregate many document hashes into a Merkle tree and commit only the root to Bitcoin via OP_RETURN (one tx anchors thousands)
Two steps: stamp yields an incomplete .ots with PendingAttestation(calendar URL); upgrade adds BitcoinBlockHeaderAttestation
.ots is an ordered path of operations: append/prepend <hex> and hash ops (sha256, ripemd160)
Verification replays ops from the document hash up to the Bitcoin block Merkle root / header
Completed proof is self-contained: needs only file + .ots + trusted Bitcoin block headers
